passage:
"Madhav, did you eat a biscuit?"
Madhav, two, stood by the open tin, chocolate crumbs all over his chin. "No biscuit."
"No?" said his mother, Gurleen, trying not to smile.
He shook his head hard. More crumbs fell. "No biscuit, Mumma."
Gurleen knelt and wiped his chin. "Look, crumbs! You ate one. That's okay. One more after lunch."
Madhav looked at the cloth, then at her, surprised. "Crumbs," he said, and giggled.

qa.q: What was all over Madhav's chin?
qa.a: Chocolate crumbs were all over his chin.

qa.q: What does Madhav's "No biscuit" suggest he wants?
qa.a: It suggests he hopes saying no will make the biscuit trouble go away; he doesn't realise his mother can see the crumbs.

qa.q: How did Gurleen respond in a helpful way?
qa.a: She stayed calm, gently showed him the crumbs, said it was okay, and set a simple rule for after lunch.

qa.q: How does Gurleen see Madhav's "No biscuit"?
qa.a: She finds it sweet and funny, trying not to smile, because she knows he isn't being sneaky, just hopeful.

grounding: A toddler with crumbs on his face says 'no biscuit' as a hopeful reflex, not cunning, unaware that his mother can see what he did.

passage:
Daycare note, Monday.
Eshaan (2½) drew a long green line along the wall by the sandpit. When I asked, "What happened to the wall?" he hid the crayon behind his back and said, "Not me." The crayon was still poking out. He looked at me hopefully.
I said, "Crayons go on paper," and gave him a wet cloth. He scrubbed happily. I will tell his parents it is typical for his age.
Dilnaz

qa.q: Where did Eshaan draw the green line?
qa.a: Along the wall by the sandpit.

qa.q: What does Eshaan's hopeful look suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he hoped saying "Not me" would be enough, without understanding that Dilnaz could already see the crayon.

qa.q: What did Dilnaz do that helped?
qa.a: Dilnaz didn't treat it as a lie, calmly said crayons go on paper, and let him help wipe the wall.

qa.q: What will Eshaan's parents learn from the note?
qa.a: They will learn that this kind of denial is typical at his age and needs calm guidance, not worry about cunning.

grounding: A daycare worker sees a toddler deny drawing on the wall while holding the crayon, a hopeful reflex from a child who cannot yet model what the adult knows.

passage:
Papa Deepak came back from the balcony. The biscuit tin was open on the floor. Little Pankaj sat beside it, chocolate crumbs all over his cheeks.
"Pankaj, did you eat a biscuit?"
Pankaj shook his head hard. "No biccit!" He smiled a big hopeful smile. Crumbs fell off his chin.
Papa bit his lip so he wouldn't laugh. He wiped Pankaj's face gently. "Next time, ask Papa, okay?"
Pankaj nodded and pointed at the tin. "More?"

qa.q: What was on Pankaj's cheeks?
qa.a: Chocolate crumbs were all over his cheeks.

qa.q: Why did Pankaj say "No biccit" with a big smile?
qa.a: Pankaj felt hopeful that saying no would make it true, not realising Papa could see the crumbs.

qa.q: How did Papa respond well?
qa.a: Papa stayed calm, wiped his face gently and taught him to ask next time, instead of scolding the denial.

qa.q: How might Papa feel seeing the crumbs and the "No biccit"?
qa.a: Papa feels amused and fond, biting his lip so he wouldn't laugh.

grounding: It shows a toddler with crumbs on his face saying no biscuit as a hopeful reflex, not cunning.

passage:
"Urmila, where did the laddoo go?" Amma asked.
"No laddoo!"
"No?" Amma knelt down. There was sugar on Urmila's chin and a yellow crumb on her frock.
"No!" Urmila hid her hands behind her back and grinned.
Cousin Ishita, sitting on the sofa, giggled.
"Hmm," said Amma, smiling. "I think a laddoo walked into your tummy."
Urmila giggled too and patted her tummy. "Laddoo in there."
"Next time, you ask Amma, okay?"
"Okay!"

qa.q: What was on Urmila's chin?
qa.a: There was sugar on Urmila's chin.

qa.q: Why did Urmila hide her hands and grin?
qa.a: Urmila felt hopeful and playful, as if hiding her hands and saying no would make the laddoo disappear.

qa.q: What did Amma do that suits a toddler's denial?
qa.a: Amma stayed light and playful, turned it into a joke about the laddoo in her tummy, and reminded her to ask next time.

qa.q: How does Ishita react to Urmila's "No laddoo"?
qa.a: Ishita finds it funny and giggles, seeing the sugar that Urmila doesn't realise everyone can see.

grounding: It shows a toddler with sugar on her chin saying no laddoo, a hopeful reflex that does not yet understand what the adult can see.

passage:
Daycare note, Room 2, Thursday.
At snack time, Tushar took Lakshmi's chocolate from her tray while she was looking at the fish tank. When I came over, his mouth and fingers were brown.
"Tushar, did you eat Lakshmi's chocolate?"
"No choco," he said, shaking his head very seriously.
Lakshmi started to cry. I wiped Tushar's hands and said, "Chocolate on your fingers. Let's give Lakshmi a hug and share your banana."
He did. He is still too little to know I can see what he sees.

qa.q: Where was Lakshmi looking when Tushar took her chocolate?
qa.a: She was looking at the fish tank.

qa.q: What did Tushar hope when he said "No choco"?
qa.a: Tushar felt hopeful that saying no would make the problem go away, without knowing the caregiver could see the chocolate.

qa.q: How did the caregiver handle it?
qa.a: The caregiver named what was seen calmly, wiped his hands and helped him make it right with a hug and his banana.

qa.q: How did Lakshmi feel when her chocolate was gone?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt upset and started to cry.

grounding: A caregiver notes a toddler with chocolate on his fingers saying no chocolate, a hopeful reflex rather than cunning.

passage:
In the courtyard of their house in Tezpur, Parveen came back from hanging the washing and found the biscuit tin open. Two-year-old Bhupen sat beside it, cheeks full, crumbs all down his vest.
"Bhupen, did you eat the biscuits?"
He shook his head hard. "No biscuit." A crumb fell off his chin.
Parveen bit back a laugh. She knelt and brushed his vest. "Biscuits are yummy, na? Next time, ask Ma first." Bhupen nodded and held out a sticky hand for one more.

qa.q: Where were the crumbs?
qa.a: All down his vest.

qa.q: Why did Bhupen shake his head and say 'No biscuit'?
qa.a: Bhupen felt a little worried about trouble and hoped saying no would make it so; he couldn't yet imagine that Ma could see the crumbs.

qa.q: How did Parveen respond, and why does it suit a two-year-old?
qa.a: She held back a laugh, brushed off the crumbs, and kindly said to ask Ma next time, since at two the denial is a hopeful reflex, not cunning.

qa.q: What would change if Parveen scolded him for lying?
qa.a: Bhupen would be confused and frightened, since at two he doesn't understand lying yet, and might only learn to fear being found out.

grounding: Shows a toddler with crumbs on his face saying 'no biscuit', a hopeful reflex rather than cunning.
